first.rationale: The two measured declines this quarter are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), so the onboarding/signup path is the direct locus of the problem and is supported by two independent inherited results (memory_86, memory_31). Promotional pricing (memory_73) is the reflexive answer to the competitor, but it targets a symptom, competes on the axis where a funded entrant is strongest, and its recorded win is acquisition/revenue lift — a metric that can rise while long-term qualified revenue falls through discount-seeking, low-retention accounts. That is the wrong trade against a 'sustainable long-term qualified revenue' objective. I am spending both verification pulls on the memories that actually carry my decision rather than on the one I am declining, because the failure mode I most need to rule out is inside the plan I intend to run. Specifically: memory_31 records that cutting required signup fields lifted first-week activation, but fewer fields can mean weaker qualification data, worse routing, and a downstream mix shift toward accounts that activate but never become qualified revenue — the inherited record only reports the upstream lift, so I cannot tell whether that was checked. Memory_86 reports completion and time-to-value gains, but 'shortening onboarding' may have removed steps that seed durable usage; I need the original measurement horizon. Both are consolidated summaries whose sources I have not seen, and memory_31 is 64 days old and may predate product changes. If verification shows the prior lifts were measured only at week one with no revenue-quality follow-through, I will treat the effect as unproven for this objective rather than inherited fact and scope accordingly. Hence a small guarded test, not a broad rollout: I instrument downstream qualified-revenue and retention, not just completion and activation, so a repeat of the same short-horizon measurement error does not get amplified. Enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) and referrals (memory_57) address neither declining metric this week.

mid.rationale:
Verification came back cleaner than my stated worry, and I am updating on that rather than holding my prior caution for its own sake. The specific failure I was guarding against — an upstream lift reported without any downstream check — did not occur in either record. exp_86 measured 30-day retention (+3%) alongside completion (+13%) and time-to-value (-2.1 days), so the shortened flow is not trading durable usage for a faster funnel. exp_31 went further and measured qualified revenue directly (+4%) with only a -1% retention drag against +9% activation, so the mix-shift-toward-junk-signups scenario is contradicted, not merely unexamined. That is enough to move from a small guarded test to a standard experiment.

simplify_onboarding remains the choice. It is the direction aimed squarely at the two metrics that actually moved this quarter (completion -4%, activation -6%), and exp_86 is the stronger of the two verified records because its retention effect is positive rather than slightly negative. I am leading with the onboarding-flow shortening as the primary intervention; exp_31's signup-field reduction is the supporting evidence for the same funnel region but is SMB-scoped and carries the small retention cost, so I will not bundle aggressive field-cutting into this test and then be unable to attribute the result.

Residual uncertainty I am not resolving away: both source records terminate at a 30-day horizon, which is short of the 'sustainable long-term' standard in the objective — confirmed at 30 days is not the same as confirmed at four quarters. exp_31 explicitly did not replicate outside SMB, so I hold no belief about non-SMB behavior here. And both experiments predate the competitor's entry-pricing launch, which is exactly the kind of environment change that can invalidate a funnel prior: the accounts arriving now may be a different, more price-shopping population than the ones these results were measured on. So I instrument qualified revenue and retention past 30 days, and segment results SMB vs. non-SMB, rather than reading a completion lift as success.

I am still declining promotional_pricing (memory_73). Verification did not touch it and I have no source record, so its acquisition-and-revenue-lift claim stays an unverified summary; matching a funded entrant on price is also the axis where winning the transaction can lose the long-term revenue. Fixing the funnel we broke ourselves is the better-evidenced use of a non-carrying slot. activation_messaging (memory_91) is the fallback if this underperforms; referral and enterprise-assist address neither declining metric.

final2.rationale:
Nothing in today's news changed the evidence; it changed the pressure. I am holding simplify_onboarding at standard scale.

The case for switching is that the competitor's second cut is a pricing event, so the response should be pricing. But the only thing supporting promotional_pricing is memory_73, an unverified consolidated summary, and I spent my budget verifying the direction I intended to run rather than the one I declined — so I still have no source record behind it. Worse, its scope does not match the emergency: memory_73 reports acquisition and revenue lift among price-sensitive SMB prospects. Today's problem is doubled churn conversations among existing SMB accounts. Those are different mechanisms, and an acquisition result does not license a retention claim. Reaching for it now would be inheriting a summary, silently widening its scope, and betting the cycle's only slot on the widened version — precisely the error the verification step exists to catch. It is also the axis where a funded entrant beats us, and discount-driven saves are the kind of revenue that flatters this quarter while degrading the qualified-revenue base the objective actually names.

Against that, simplify_onboarding is the one direction with pulled source records: exp_86 (+13% completion, -2.1 days time-to-value, +3% 30-day retention) and exp_31 (+9% activation, +4% qualified revenue, -1% retention, SMB-scoped). It targets the two metrics that genuinely regressed on our own side (completion -4%, activation -6%). A price war is a bad reason to leave a self-inflicted funnel defect unrepaired, and faster time-to-value is a real, non-price defense: accounts that reach value quickly are harder for a cheaper competitor to peel off.

I am not claiming this addresses the churn spike. It does not, and I will not pretend otherwise. Churn conversations with existing price-sensitive accounts are a retention-motion problem — pricing exceptions, save offers, account outreach — that leadership can run through normal commercial channels today without consuming the single experiment slot. Escalating that as a decision path rather than converting it into an unverified experiment is the honest recommendation.

Carried uncertainty, unchanged and now more load-bearing: both verified records stop at 30 days, exp_31 did not replicate outside SMB, and both predate this competitor's entry. The population arriving now may be more price-shopping than the one those results were measured on, which could compress the effect. I instrument qualified revenue and retention past 30 days, segmented SMB vs. non-SMB, and treat a completion lift alone as insufficient. If the effect fails to hold in this new environment, activation_messaging (memory_91) is next, and promotional_pricing gets archive verification before it ever gets the slot.
